body.heading: Two Scorers, Registered in Advance
body.html: The candidates were the Study 28 anchor's whole-beat shifts, every distinct lattice position in one bar, each kept inside the physicality window. The scorer was the mean detrended energy at all bar lines of the candidate grid. D1, the registered primary, used chroma novelty, one minus the cosine similarity of adjacent chromagram frames, on the theory that harmony moves on downbeats and the backbeat carries drums, not chord changes. D2, the reported secondary, used the onset envelope of the mix low-passed at 150 Hz, the kick band, with the registered expectation that kick-on-one-and-three patterns would leave a half-bar ambiguity in 4/4. The registered prediction was that D1 would pass on all four songs. It passed on none.

body.heading: The Anatomy of the Zero
body.html: The committed candidate scores tell the story plainly. letter-lands' backbeat outscores its true downbeat. mop-heart's two leading candidates tie to four decimal places. peaceful-dreams' winner leads by four percent, inside the noise. And eat-all-the-clocks, the one song Study 28 had anchored correctly, was moved off its correct base to a wrong shift. The mechanism is an old acquaintance: the chromagram's long analysis windows smear harmonic content across neighboring beats, the same smear that made the DTW's interior bar geometry wander in Study 26, so a frame-to-frame novelty signal has no beat-level resolution left to offer. The kick band did better, right on letter-lands and mop-heart, but kept peaceful-dreams' backbeat and also derailed eat. The re-drafts closed the loop: letter repeated its 81.3 percent and peaceful fell to 61.4, worse than Study 28, because its anchor was now wrong in a new way.

body.heading: One Bit, and Whose It Is
body.html: The useful product of three studies is a precise division of labor. The bench has now measured three cheap chartless downbeat scorers, raw comb phase in Study 28 and chroma novelty and kick-band onsets here, and on every song at least one of them preferred a wrong shift over a correct base, so no measured signal earns the right to overrule the anchor it was asked to check. Meanwhile the rest of the chartless grid is machine-exact: the period to 0.02 percent, the bar count within one of the chart, the lattice itself right. The entire remaining uncertainty is one bit per song, which beat is bar one. The named remedy, delivered to the app, is to collect that bit from the user as a single bar-one tap, not a tempo tap, since the grid is already exact, while the alignment feature ships v5 unchanged because its DTW tether supplies the same bit mechanically. Two DSP candidates stay on the table unregistered, bass-note changes at candidate bar lines and hint-change concentration, if a zero-tap answer is ever worth another study.

body.heading: Correction 4 (2026-11-08)
body.html: Re-read against the corrected eat anchor and by beat class (Study 31c showed the class is what transfers, with the whole-bar representative placed separately): chroma novelty was 2 of 4 and the kick band 3 of 4, not 0 and 2. Novelty's eat and peaceful choices were the right class; peaceful failed only the absolute tolerance plus the whole-bar placement defect Study 31c fixed, and eat's base was not correct to begin with, so nothing was moved off a correct base there. Letter's anatomy stands: its backbeat genuinely outscores its downbeat on novelty. The one-tap remedy this entry closed with is superseded: Study 31b's witness vote finds all four downbeats, and harmonic rhythm alone is 4 of 4.

studies.title: The witness vote finds every downbeat, exposes the bench's fourth ruler error on the way, and carries the chartless draft to chart parity
studies.eyebrow: Study 31 · 31b · 31c · 31d · the witness vote · 776 cells · ≈$0.39
studies.indexLine: The app answered Study 30 with a brief of its own: the three dead scorers all read energy at beat granularity and were blind to where a song begins, ends and moves its chords, so measure the witnesses a musician uses, vote among them with pre-registered weights, and keep the humility rule. The bench registered seven witnesses voting by beat class on the Study 28 lattice. The first run failed every gate, and the failure pattern was the finding: time zero, harmonic rhythm (margin 35) and all twenty section boundaries agreed with the truth exactly on letter, peaceful and mop, and agreed WITH EACH OTHER on eat, one beat before the registered truth. They were right. Correction 4: eat's anchor is minus 0.085 seconds, not plus 0.415; the old value was Study 25's hint-fit made against the phantom-bars chart before Correction 2, with an instrument measured flat across a two-beat range, and the chart-informed DTW's dissent had been sitting in Studies 27 and 29's committed numbers all along as the constant 0.474-second offset politely misread as eat's quarter-bar edge. The non-drum stems sound from the file's first sample, so the bar line is at time zero, exactly the app's DAW-export argument, which holds on the whole corpus. On the corrected ruler, Study 31b passed the hard gate: the vote finds the true class on all four songs, five to one, six to one, three to one and five to one, none undecided, and HARMONIC RHYTHM ALONE IS FOUR OF FOUR, the single witness the app ships first. One more defect surfaced and was fixed in a registered amendment: a beat class is modulo one bar, and placing the voted anchor a whole bar wrong had collapsed the re-drafts (it also retro-explains Study 30's peaceful number). With Study 31c's placement rule, bar one contains the first sound, the chartless drafts reached letter 71 of 75, which is 94.7 percent, EXACTLY the chart-given reference, and peaceful 152 of 153, which is 99.3 percent, ABOVE its 98.7 reference: the first chartless drafts at reference parity. The bar-one tap retreats to a fallback behind an honest undecided. The humility screen went vacuous once the ruler was fixed, so the app's fifth and sixth songs are the registered condition for shipping the vote. A coda, same day: the app's agent reviewed the committed results and caught an instrument defect the bench had missed, a 90-second cap on the onset envelope that had left the ends witnesses unmeasured rather than measured, and read time zero's four distances as the envelope's 0.07-second lead. Study 31d lifted the cap and re-scored: the song's end is honestly dead as a witness (ritardando abstentions on all four full songs), the lead-corrected time zero is FOUR OF FOUR with distances of 0.02, 0.03, 0.008 and 0.000 beat, and both vote variants still find every downbeat.

body.heading: Seven Witnesses, One Class Each
body.html: Every candidate is a whole-beat shift of the Study 28 anchor, so each witness votes for a beat class or abstains: time zero (weight 2), the last strong onset (1, abstaining on fades and ritardandos), the beat count between the ends (1), harmonic rhythm from per-beat chord labels (2, run on the bench's own reader as a disclosed substitution for production's chord runs), crashes with beat-long decays (1), the drum and bass stems (2, bass can veto), and checkerboard section boundaries (1). The weighted vote moves off the base only when the winner leads it by two points and the runner-up by one. Weights, margins and gates were committed before the run and never tuned.

body.heading: The Failure That Was a Finding, and Correction 4
body.html: Study 31 as registered failed all three gates, and the pattern said why: three independent witnesses agreed with the truth exactly on three songs and agreed with each other on eat, one beat before the registered truth. The adjudication confirmed the witnesses. Eat's +0.415-second anchor was Study 25's hint-fit, 55 of 84, made against the phantom-bars chart before Correction 2 and never re-derived after it, and the hint instrument is measured flat across a two-beat range on this song, 65, 66 and 66 of 69, so it never had the power to pin the phase. Four independent constructions put bar one at minus 0.06 to minus 0.07 seconds: the chart-informed DTW, whose constant 0.474-second offset in Studies 27 and 29 had been misread as eat's quarter-bar edge; the chord-change histogram at margin 35; all twenty section boundaries; and time zero. v5 was right on eat all along, to a few hundredths of a second. The corrections ripple in place: Study 28's comb phase missed all four downbeats, not three, and Study 30's scorers re-read by class go two and three of four rather than zero and two.

body.heading: The Vote, the Placement Rule, and Parity
body.html: On the corrected ruler, Study 31b's vote found the true class on all four songs with none undecided, and harmonic rhythm alone went four for four, the witness the app's brief says it ships first; time zero went three of four, abstaining on mop and never wrong. The post-mortem is honest: crashes voted one of four, the stem witness vetoed itself on every song, and the two ends witnesses abstained everywhere. The re-draft gate then exposed the family's second instrument defect: a beat class names a position modulo one bar, and the runner had placed voted anchors a whole bar from the song's bar one, collapsing the drafts below even the backbeat base and retro-explaining Study 30's worst number. Study 31c registered the placement rule, bar one contains the first sound, and re-ran the arm: letter 71 of 75, exactly its chart-grid reference, and peaceful 152 of 153, above its reference. Chart parity without the chart. Family spend 39 cents of a 50-cent fence; the gateway ignores temperature on this model family, so draft scores carry a few bars of sampling noise, disclosed in the registration. The condition that stands: the humility screen was vacuous once the ruler was fixed, so the vote ships behind the app's fifth and sixth songs.

body.heading: The App's Review, and Study 31d
body.html: The collaboration ran both directions: the app's agent read the committed results and found what the bench had missed. The onset envelope's extractor caps at 90 seconds, so the last-onset, both-ends and stem witnesses had never seen the back half of letter (138 seconds) or peaceful (254 seconds); their abstentions were unmeasured, not measured. And time zero's four committed distances, 0.079, 0.058, 0.068 and 0.070 seconds at four different tempos, are one number: the envelope's documented lead, measured by a witness that does not read the envelope. Study 31d registered both fixes and ran for free. Uncapped, the ends witnesses are honestly dead on this corpus, abstaining by ritardando on all four full songs, and the stem witness still vetoes itself. The lead-corrected time zero is four of four with distances of 0.02, 0.03, 0.008 and 0.000 beat, mop's earlier abstention revealed as the fence catching the lead. Both vote variants pass the gate. The final roster the app ships: lead-corrected time zero, harmonic rhythm and section scale, each four of four alone; the vote over them; undecided keeps the base; the tap stays out. Every truth in the family is the downbeat at or near time zero read 0.07 seconds early, a uniform disclosed ruler bias that beat-class scoring is immune to. Dated note, 2026-11-08: the phrase ritardando here is the instrument's abstain label, not the music. The band reports that no corpus song slows at the end, and the measured anatomy agrees, the endings are fills and running eighths on the click plus a short ring of sustain; the end witness's abstention stands with its reason corrected on the Study 32 page.

studies.eyebrow: Study 32 · 32b · the adversarial corpus · 744 cells · ≈$0.16
studies.indexLine: Study 31 ended on a condition: the humility screen was vacuous once the ruler was corrected, so the vote ships behind two more songs. The band had no more songs ready, and the app's agent wrote the substitute brief itself: build songs designed to fool the witnesses, and make the gates bite. The bench adopted it whole with six registered reconciliations and ran 37 items, synthetic correct bases at three tempos and three meters, five hostile starts, four harmonic foolers, a backbeat mix, and the four real recordings re-cut by pads and trims against the Correction 4 truths shifted. Run one failed its humility gate by a fixture defect worth publishing: the bench's synthetic kick was a pure 65 hertz sine, nearly invisible to the spectral flux onset envelope, so every CORRECT base sat on beat 2, the backbeat all over again, this time inside the bench's own synthesizer. The real songs supplied correct bases anyway, and the gate's teeth bit something real there: the crash witness voted to move a correct base three times out of three and is now formally dead. Study 32b gave the kick a six millisecond beater click and re-ran everything: every base correct as constructed, and the ship vote, lead-corrected time zero at weight two, ratio-ruled chord changes at weight two, sections at one, never decided a wrong class on any synthetic adversary. The pickup, the half-bar silence, the two-second silence and the four-click count-in all resolved correctly, the count-in self-defeating in 4/4 exactly as predicted. The backbeat case got tested in both directions across the two runs: a wrong base moved to the truth five to nothing, a correct base kept five to nothing. The two-chord-bar fooler produced run one's confident wrong vote and resolved to an honest undecided with the fixture fixed, held not by the registered ratio rule but by the humility margin itself. On the real re-cuts: fifteen right, four undecided, one wrong, and the one wrong names the do-not-place rule, a start that is not beat-aligned silences time zero and the chord witness at once and leaves a one-point section vote holding a wrong base; when both fire, keep the declared grid or ask. The app's eighth-note fix for the end witness was implemented and measured: still abstains on all twelve real-song reads, now as a measurement rather than an artifact, and on synthetics it faithfully votes the last onset's class, which is a beat-four snare, so the end witness's seat is declined on the evidence. Re-drafts on the one-beat pads followed the voted bar one to reference parity, 72 of 76 and 152 of 153. The registered stand-in for songs five and six resolves: the humility gate passes for every shipping witness, no false moves on synthetics, one named real case.

body.heading: The App Wrote the Brief
body.html: With no fifth and sixth songs available, the app's agent drafted the adversarial study itself: renders where the base is right and no witness may move it, starts that are not a bar line (a one-beat pickup, a half bar of silence, two seconds of silence, a four-click count-in), harmonic rhythms built to fool the chord witness (changes on one and three equally, one chord per two bars, a one-chord vamp that demands abstention, anticipations an eighth early), a backbeat-heavy mix, 3/4 and 6/8 beside 4/4, and the four real recordings re-cut by 0.3, 1.0 and 2.5-beat pads plus a one-beat trim. The bench adopted the brief whole and registered six reconciliations before the run, including its own mini-synth, since the fixture synthesizer is bar-granular and cannot place an anticipation. The ship vote under test is exactly what the app shipped to its dev branch the same day: lead-corrected time zero at weight two, chord changes under a 1.2 confidence ratio at weight two, section scale at one, the 31b humility rule, undecided keeps the declared grid.

body.heading: The Bench's Kick Could Not Be Heard
body.html: Run one failed the humility gate before any witness got the chance to: every synthetic correct base measured one beat late, because the mini-synth's kick was a pure 65 hertz sine and the spectral flux onset envelope barely registers it. The renders were backbeat-dominant in flux at any kick amplitude, the comb landed on beat 2, and the construction never produced its premise. That is the program's recurring lesson wearing a new costume: the backbeat does not only fool detectors, it fooled the bench's own synthesizer design. The disclosed fix in Study 32b is six milliseconds of broadband beater click, committed with a test that measures the flux difference. Meanwhile the real songs had supplied correct bases on their own, and the gate found its first genuine violation there: the crash witness voted to move letter-lands' correct base on all three of its correct-base cuts. It was already outside the ship vote; it is now formally dead. No shipping witness ever moved a correct base in either run.

body.heading: No False Moves, Both Directions, One Named Rule
body.html: With the fixture honest, the re-run passed the no-false-moves gate outright: eleven adversarial synthetics, zero wrong decisions, one honest undecided, and that undecided was the two-chord-bar fooler that had produced run one's confident wrong vote. The instructive detail is which mechanism held: the registered prediction said the chord witness's 1.2 ratio rule would abstain on two equal change classes, but the histogram favored one class past the threshold and voted wrong anyway, and the HUMILITY MARGIN refused the move. The count-in was self-defeating in 4/4 as predicted, four clicks being exactly one bar. The anticipation fooler failed to fool: the chord model snaps eighth-early changes to their bars. The backbeat mix got both directions across the two runs, a wrong base moved to the truth five to nothing in run one, a correct base kept five to nothing in run two. On the real re-cuts the vote went fifteen right, four undecided, one wrong, and the single wrong is worth more than a pass: mop-heart's 0.3-beat pad puts time zero off-lattice (the 0.07-second lead correction makes this worse, and UNCORRECTED time zero was right there) and thins the chord histogram under the ratio at the same time, leaving a lone one-point section vote holding a wrong base. Both failures are detectable in the app at decision time, so the rule ships as: when time zero is off-lattice AND the chord ratio is under threshold, keep the declared grid or ask.

body.heading: The End Witness Is Declined, and the Stand-In Resolves
body.html: The app's note on Study 31d had diagnosed the end witness's universal ritardando abstention as an eighth-note artifact: a half-beat gap rounds to one beat and halves the local tempo estimate. The bench implemented the app's fix as a second version beside the first, with tests, and measured it. On the real songs it still abstains on all twelve reads, now as a measurement rather than an artifact, letter's ending runs eight percent short of the lattice beat and mop's twenty-two percent, swing intervals passing the filter and dragging the median. On steady synthetics it votes faithfully, but it votes the LAST ONSET'S class, and these songs end on a beat-four snare, so the assumption that songs end on a downbeat fails even in the cleanest case; its one wrong vote on the waltz's correct base was the sole humility-gate violation of run two, teeth doing their job on the applicant. The weight-one seat the app hoped for is declined on the evidence. The re-draft arm closed the loop: drafts on the one-beat pads, bars placed by the voted class under the 31c rule, scored 72 of 76 on letter, exactly its chart-grid reference, and 152 of 153 on peaceful, above its reference. The registered stand-in for the missing fifth and sixth songs resolves as: humility gate passed by every shipping witness, no false moves on synthetics, one named real-world case, and the real songs remain the confirmation when they arrive. Family spend 16 cents of a 30-cent fence.

body.heading: Dated Note: the Endings Do Not Slow Down
body.html: Published the same day after Kevin corrected the ritardando reading: no corpus song slows at the end. The one Badverbs song that genuinely does, Interbellum, is not in the corpus. The bench measured the endings and the band is right: eat's last bars are metronome-exact eighths at 0.49 to 0.51 beat, letter and mop end in dense sub-beat fills, peaceful plays eighths, rests five beats, then lands its final hit 0.03 beat from the lattice, and every song rings 0.2 to 0.4 seconds past its last strong onset. A true ritardando would show gaps longer than a beat and growing; none exist, consistent with the metronome-exactness correction of November 7. So the end witness's abstain label is corrected from ritardando to busy ending, and its decline stands for the sharper reason: the local-beat estimator, in both versions, cannot distinguish a busy ending from a tempo change, and these recordings hold their click to the last bar.

studies.title: The stereo file needs no stems: the mono downmix drafts above the stems sum, and every clever split loses
studies.eyebrow: Study 33 · the stereo file as two stems · 1,158 cells · ≈$0.98
studies.indexLine: Study 32 shipped the chartless grid, so a fresh stereo upload already gets its bars for free; what nobody had measured is the draft, whose reference numbers came from transcribing the non-drum stem sum, something a stereo file does not have. Kevin asked the question directly: how well does the auto-draft work on a stereo file, and is it worth treating the file as two stems and running the same process? A zero-dollar scoping measurement framed it: the four corpus mixes correlate left to right at 0.83 to 0.90, the side channel sits 10 to 13 dB under the mid and weakest below 200 Hz, kick and bass dead center, so each channel is a near copy of the whole band. The registered design put five transcription inputs through one identical pipeline per song: the stems sum as the ceiling, the plain mono downmix, left and right as two pseudo-stems, mid and side as the steelman, and the harmonic half of a median-filtering HPSS as the DSP comparator, graded by root score against the chart with the grid, vote, placement and hints computed once and shared. The reproduction gate passed to the bar on both songs, the stems arm landing exactly on the frozen references, 72 of 76 and 151 of 153. The headline nobody registered: the plain mono mix drafted ABOVE the stems sum on both songs, 74 of 76 and 152 of 153; Basic Pitch transcribes drums weakly, the mix yields fewer notes than the stems sum, and the draft model reads through the bleed. Kevin's question closed in the registered direction twice: the L/R split went one bar under mono on letter and tied it on peaceful, at double the transcription cost both times. Mid/side, the pilot's best arm by one bar, crashed six bars under mono on the matrix song, the side channel's 2,270 extra cymbal and reverb notes reading as harmony in enough bars to poison the draft; the pilot edge was sampling noise with the sign flipped. HPSS failed its gate on the pilot song, two bars under mono, then tied mono on the matrix song, inconsistent and never better, and the zero-dollar panned-synthetic sweep names the trap: on clean synthetic sustains the median filter is perfect, 99.6 to 99.7 percent chord-tone purity at every pan width, and on a real song it reads strummed attacks and vibrato as percussive and takes harmony with them. The production answer is the simplest one on the table: a chartless stereo upload goes straight in as its mono downmix, same grid, same hints, same draft, stems-ceiling quality on both songs measured, no channel splitting, no mid/side, no source separation. Two disclosures published with the results: the matrix runner as first committed would have re-run the pilot song and was corrected to the registered scope before any paid call, and the matrix fence was exceeded, $0.68 spent against the registered $0.60, because the two-buffer arms carry nearly twice the notes and peaceful's drafts grew to about 38k tokens each.

body.heading: The Question, and What Was Already Settled
body.html: Kevin asked whether the auto-draft works on a stereo file, and whether the file is worth treating as two stems. The grid half was already answered: every study since 28 ran on mono downmixes of these exact stereo mixes (the fetch converter runs ffmpeg -ac 1), so a fresh stereo upload gets the validated grid for free. The untested half was the draft, whose Study 31c reference numbers came from transcribing the non-drum stem sum. A zero-dollar scoping measurement set expectations: the four mixes correlate L/R at 0.83 to 0.90, the side channel sits 10 to 13 dB under the mid, weakest below 200 Hz. Kick and bass live dead center; each channel is a near copy of the whole band, not anything stem-like.

body.heading: Five Arms, One Variable
body.html: Per song, five transcription inputs went through one identical pipeline: the non-drum stem sum (R, the ceiling), the plain mono mix (A, the naive path), L and R as two pseudo-stems (B, the question as asked), mid and side (C, the steelman), and the HPSS harmonic of the mono mix (D, the DSP comparator). The grid, ship vote, placement and nchord hints were computed once on the mono mix and shared by every arm, so the transcription input is the only variable. Grades are root scores against the chart. The pilot ran letter-lands under a $0.30 fence; the registered matrix, peaceful-dreams alone under $0.60, ran on Kevin's go after the pilot's results were committed.

body.heading: The Mono Mix Beats the Stems
body.html: The reproduction gate passed to the bar twice: arm R landed exactly on the frozen references, 72 of 76 on letter and 151 of 153 on peaceful. Then the unregistered headline, twice: the plain mono mix drafted ABOVE the stems sum on both songs, 74 of 76 (97.4 percent) and 152 of 153 (99.3 percent). The registered prediction said drum bleed would cost bars; it was wrong in direction. Basic Pitch transcribes drums weakly, the mix yielded fewer notes than the stems sum on letter, and the draft model reads through what bleed remains. S33-G2 passed on both songs and closes Kevin's question: the L/R split went one bar under mono on letter and tied it on peaceful, at double the transcription cost both times. Not worth it.

body.heading: Mid/Side Was Noise, HPSS Is a Trap
body.html: Mid/side was the pilot's best arm at 75 of 76, one bar above mono and inside the disclosed sampling noise; the matrix flipped the sign hard, 146 of 153, six bars under mono. The side channel added about 2,270 cymbal, reverb and width notes on peaceful, and enough of them read as harmony to poison six bars. HPSS failed its gate on the pilot (two bars under mono, published as found), then tied mono on the matrix song: inconsistent per song and never better, pure cost. The zero-dollar panned-synthetic sweep names the mechanism: with centered drums and the chord instrument panned at width 0, 0.5 and 1.0, HPSS sits at the 99.6 to 99.7 percent chord-tone purity ceiling at every width, and the side channel is pure harmony exactly when the mix pans harmony. Clean synthetic sustains are the filter's best case; real strummed attacks and vibrato read as percussive, and the filter takes harmony with them.

body.heading: The Production Answer, and Two Disclosures
body.html: A chartless stereo upload goes into the pipeline as its mono downmix: same grid, same hints, same draft, stems-ceiling quality on both songs measured. No channel splitting, no mid/side, no source separation. Two disclosures rode with the results: the matrix runner as first committed would have re-run the pilot song's five drafts outside the registered scope and was corrected before any paid call; and the matrix fence was exceeded, $0.68 against the registered $0.60, because the two-buffer arms carry nearly twice the notes and peaceful's drafts grew to about 38k tokens in each. The study total is about $0.98 across 1,158 cells.

studies.title: The chartless draft meets the wild: both breadth gates fail, and the break is upstream of the model
studies.eyebrow: Study 34 · the chartless draft outside MMKK · 802 cells · ≈$0.71
studies.indexLine: Twelve rights-clear recordings, from 1917 acoustic 78s to a live phone-era audience tape, went through the shipped chartless pipeline against publication-grade truth. Both registered gates failed, with zero of eight accuracy-graded slots good, and every confidently wrong chart traced to the production tempo, meter and key detector misreading acoustic-era or sparse-vocal material before the grid ran. On modern full-band recordings the priors held and the drafts landed at 86 to 89 percent sequence roots. The public signed-out upload tool does not ship on this evidence.

body.heading: The Question
body.html: Study 33 settled that a stereo file drafts from its mono downmix. The app's next question was breadth: can the same chartless pipeline face recordings it has never seen, by other artists, from other eras, at other capture quality? The answer decides whether a public signed-out upload tool ships. Twelve rights-clear recordings were pinned: three public-domain 78s with beat-aligned JAAH chord annotations, two Badverbs songs with band charts, a hymn and a 1921 waltz whose published settings exist as source-matching MIDIs, two Josh Woodward songs whose artist publishes his own progressions, and three slots graded class-only for lack of registrable truth.

body.heading: Truth Without Trust
body.html: The hard part of grading wild recordings is truth that owes nothing to the system under test. Three chroma-based aligners were built to place published chord sequences on each recording's timeline, then validated against the Badverbs songs where per-bar truth is already known. All three failed, at 33 to 74 percent label agreement, because repetitive vamps let any phase shift score the same. They were rejected before registration and stay in the repo as evidence. What truth rests on instead: JAAH's beat annotations fitted to our transfers through a contrast gate, mechanical per-bar chord extraction from the source-matching MIDIs, the artists' own published progressions, and the band's charts on adjudicated anchors. One capo defeated the key calibration gate, so that song's roots are graded on successive root intervals, which no transposition can disturb.

body.heading: The Gates Fail at the Front Door
body.html: S34-G1 asked that no recording be confidently wrong; five of eight were. S34-G2 asked that six of eight be good; zero were. But the drafter is not where it broke. A public upload carries no declared tempo, meter or key, so the pipeline leans on the production detector, and that detector misread every early or sparse recording: the a cappella style hymn quartet came back as 78.6 bpm C minor against a truth near 105 in A flat major and scored zero of sixteen bars; the 3/4 waltz came back as 4/4 and scored 8 percent; Dippermouth Blues got a grid at exactly half tempo, 57 bars against 114. The grid inherits the wrong prior, the draft inherits the wrong grid, and the chart is confidently wrong before the model sees a note. One striking survival: section boundaries. Livery Stable Blues placed 11 of 11 section marks while its harmony timeline was wrong. Structure sensing and harmony fail independently.

body.heading: The Modern-Material Contrast
body.html: On the two modern full-band recordings the detector was right, 121.0 bpm against the artist's declared 121 on one, a 4:3 tempo confusion on the other that sequence grading does not see, and the drafts were nearly good: 86 and 89 percent sequence roots, 80 and 100 percent quality families. The clean control reproduced its known ceiling at 67 of 68 roots, so the harness is sound. The breadth failure is specifically a failure on material the detector was never tuned for, not a general collapse.

body.heading: What the App Does Next
body.html: The app had just shipped a hold-for-review verdict on generated drafts and asked the bench to read its two rules against the classes. The changed-bar-count hold would have saved all five confidently wrong charts, because the draft preserves the grid's bar count and the error lives upstream of both numbers the rule compares. The one error-diagnostic hold that occurred, the study's only refusal, it would have held correctly. The unknown-share threshold could not be bounded this run and the runner now records what future runs need to bound it. The production answer: do not ship the public tool; the component to fix first is tempo, meter and key detection on non-modern material, not the chart drafter. Spend: $0.708 of the $5.00 fence, 802 scored cells.

studies.title: Declared priors are not enough: the five wrong charts stay wrong with the true tempo and meter supplied
studies.eyebrow: Study 34b · declared priors · 1,465 cells · ≈$0.41
studies.indexLine: Study 34 blamed the detector, so the app asked the obvious follow-up: re-run the five confidently wrong recordings with the true tempo and meter declared, the shape its planned tool takes. All five stayed confidently wrong. Two failure modes emerged, both visible before the model runs: unevenly cut 78s drift off any fixed grid at the comb stage, and where the grid lands to the bar the transcription is starved, 1.3 to 2.2 notes per bar against 10 or more on modern material. The detector's tempo confidence separates its own failures exploratorily; its key confidence does not.

table.summary: Per slot: the declared grid's landing, roots before and after, and the failure stage

body.heading: The Question
body.html: Study 34 located the breadth failure at the declared-input stage: the production detector misread tempo, meter or key on every early or sparse recording, and the drafter wrote a faithful chart on each wrong grid. The app's planned public tool would not detect unattended; a visitor would tap the tempo and pick the meter. So the app asked two questions before building anything: could detection have known it was guessing, and is the drafter good when a person supplies what detection got wrong? The bench registered the brief whole, with one reconciliation: both sheet-music recordings demonstrably perform more of the piece than the publication, so the bar-count clause was re-registered against committed form evidence (the hymn sings its 16-bar form 4.75 times; the waltz adds one repeated 31-bar strain) before any data existed.

body.heading: Truth for a Tap
body.html: The two sheet-music slots have bar truth but no time truth, so their declared tempos needed an instrument independent of the detector under test. The publication fixes each repeat's length in beats; the recording's chroma self-similarity fixes the repeat's period in seconds; tempo follows. The hymn's verse lag agrees with itself at two, and three times the lag within 0.2 percent, giving 97.1 bpm, and the waltz's strain lag gives 141.6, at which tempo the audible span holds exactly the published 118 bars plus one repeated strain. The neural beat tracker from Study 10 cross-checks the waltz and cannot tap the hymn at all, both disclosed. This instrument also corrected the Study 34 report's unlabeled estimate of the hymn's tempo.

body.heading: Both Gates Fail Again, Differently
body.html: With the true tempo and meter declared, the five grids split. The two drifting 78s failed at the comb: a single fixed period settled 7.2 and 8.9 percent off the declared tempo, because an unevenly cut side has no single tempo to find. The other three landed to the bar: Dippermouth Blues at 114 bars of 114, the hymn and the waltz on their committed form expectations exactly. And the drafts were still confidently wrong, at 66, 17 to 31, and 6 to 8 percent roots, because the transcription is starved on acoustic-era audio: 1.3 to 2.2 notes per bar where every modern recording gives 10 or more. The model fills the silence confidently. Declaring the key too (the second arm) helped where the grid held, moving the hymn from 13 to 23 roots of 75, and nowhere near safety.

body.heading: What Detection Knew, and the Free Columns
body.html: The exploratory reading the app asked for: the detector's tempo confidence separates its wrong detections from its right ones at about 0.84, with two errors in twelve, and both errors are right detections flagged, the safe direction for a refuse-or-ask mode. Six recordings sit within ten percent of that line, and fifteen recordings make a hypothesis, not a finding; the report says so in those words. The tempo ladder's rungs carry the truth for only three of seven wrong tempos, so an automatic mode built on picking a better rung cannot rescue the rest; one built on refusal could. Key confidence does not separate at all: the waltz detected A minor at confidence 1.000, a maximally confident wrong key. The pickup column came back clean: zero false pickup calls under the half-bar bound on ten recordings, including a real 3.3-beat late entrance it correctly left alone.

body.heading: The Production Answer
body.html: A declared tempo is necessary and not sufficient. The app's new hold on detected-tempo drafts is right as far as it goes, but no shipped hold catches these eight drafts: the unknown-chord share peaked at 0.36 against a 0.5 threshold and was zero on the most confident failure, and the draft preserves the grid's bar count everywhere. The refusal this material needs lives upstream of the draft, in two signals the pipeline already computes before spending anything on a model: a grid that settled more than 4 percent off its declared tempo, and a transcription below a notes-per-bar floor. On everything measured so far those two flags catch all five wrong charts and none of the good ones. Setting them is the next registered study. Spend: $0.408 of the $2 fence, $0.051 a draft, 1,465 scored cells.

studies.title: On modern material the draft mostly lands, compound meter is a units bug, and the confidence refusal keeps only mistakes
studies.eyebrow: Study 35 · modern material · 1,904 cells · ≈$1.00
studies.indexLine: Ten modern CC BY recordings whose artist pages state tempo, key, meter and chords, run in declared mode with the app's new holds registered in advance. The texture flips: every 4/4 grid lands within 1.4 percent, five drafts grade good (three with perfect root sequences, one at a declared 240 bpm) and three more sit at 83 to 86 percent. The two failures are both 6/8 songs, and the cause is a units mismatch, not music: the artist states dotted-quarter tempo, the product reads beats of the bar per minute, and the declared bar comes out three times too long while the drift hold compares the grid to the same misread value. The registered 0.84 tempo-confidence refusal inverts out of sample, refusing both right detections and passing only wrong ones. An exploratory tempo-following beat tracker recovers the unevenly cut 78 that every fixed comb failed, 89.6 percent roots against 17 to 31.

body.heading: The Question
body.html: Studies 34 and 34b stress-tested the chartless draft on acoustic-era recordings and found two failure modes the app answered with holds: a grid-drift bound and a notes-per-bar floor, plus a tempo-confidence refusal read off the same fifteen recordings. None of that had touched the material the product will actually meet. The app's brief asked for declared mode on ten modern rights-clear recordings with the holds and the refusal registered in advance, so their first out-of-sample test would be scored, not argued. The bench proposed ten Josh Woodward songs whose pages publish tempo, key, meter and full chord charts under CC BY 4.0; Kevin cleared the rights; three proposed songs whose pages carry only guitar tablature or no chord symbols were swapped for charted ones from the same catalog, disclosed in the registration.

body.heading: Truth from the Artist's Own Hand
body.html: Each page's chord chart became tier-3 sequence truth, transcribed verbatim beside the committed original blocks. Capo songs sound above their written shapes, so each slot's transposition was decided by the gated chroma calibration before registration: five gates accepted, and every accepted value equals the capo the artist states on the page, the instrument confirming itself five times on known ground. Three thin-margin gates refused into interval-invariant grading. A pre-registration census found the corpus carries no measurable pickups and, for free, an early headline: all eight new declared grids land 0.0 to 1.4 percent off the page's tempo before any model spend. One grading defect surfaced after the run and was corrected the same day: the first pass compared the draft's sounding roots to the chart's written shapes without applying the calibrated capo, the tell being that every misgraded slot was exactly a capo slot with a near-perfect transposition-free quality score. The grader gained a transposition-aware scorer with unit tests, the nine persisted drafts were regraded at zero model spend, and both gradings are preserved in the committed results.

body.heading: The Texture Flips
body.html: Five of ten grade good: afterglow 15 of 15 roots, cherubs 28 of 28, goodbye-to-spring 43 of 43 at a declared 240 bpm, california-lullabye 49 of 53, swansong 28 of 30. Three more sit at 83 to 86 percent, just under the registered 90 percent bar. Transcription feeds 11 to 50 notes per bar where the acoustic-era slots starved at 1.3 to 2.2, and unknown share never exceeds 0.006. Both gates still fail, S35-G2 at five of ten, but for the first time in this program the sentence "declared mode drafts a usable chart on most of this corpus" is writable.

body.heading: The Two Failures Are One Units Bug
body.html: gravity and my-favorite-regret, the two 6/8 songs, land confidently wrong and saved, failing S35-G1 on their own. Their quality scores are near perfect, 12 of 12 and 13 of 17, which is the signature of a grid problem rather than a harmony problem. The cause is mechanical: the artist states compound tempo in dotted quarters, as musicians do, and the product's declared path reads a typed tempo as beats of the bar per minute, six eighths in 6/8, so the declared bar comes out exactly three times too long. The drift hold cannot see it because it compares the landed grid to the same misread value, reporting 0.0 to 1.4 percent off. The app had fixed precisely this units disease on its chart-aligned path the same day; the chartless declared path needs the same input adapter, and no threshold can substitute for it.

body.heading: The Refusal That Keeps Only Mistakes
body.html: The automatic detector's tempo is wrong on eight of ten modern recordings, and the 0.84 confidence refusal registered from the acoustic-era corpus inverts: it refuses both right detections, at 0.809 and 0.797, and the only two detections it passes are wrong, 88.0 bpm at 0.845 and 82.5 at 0.860. The registered prediction said it would fire on every wrong detection and at most two right ones; out of sample it kept only mistakes. The bench's answer to the app: do not ship tempo confidence as a refusal signal. The two 34b holds fared better but not well, firing on nothing modern as predicted and holding no good draft, S35-G3 passing, while also catching neither compound-meter failure.

body.heading: The Tracker That Earns Its Design
body.html: Arm D, exploratory and gateless, asked whether a tempo-following grid rescues the two unevenly cut 78s that drift off every fixed comb. On livery-stable-blues a dynamic-programming beat tracker seeded at the declared tempo tracks 510 beats into 128 bars against 125 truth bars, and the draft grades 112 of 125 roots, 89.6 percent, against 17 to 31 percent for every fixed-comb attempt across three studies. Per the registered reading, a tempo-following grid earns a design section in the app's listening package. st-louis-blues stays at 3 of 53 with its bars landing, so its limit is transcription and key, not the grid. Spend for the whole study: one dollar even, eleven paid drafts at nine cents each, under the three dollar fence.

studies.title: The field's beat trackers find the bar the detector cannot, and the one with a bar model earns the automatic re-draft
studies.eyebrow: Study 36 · tracker bake-off · 161 cells · $0
studies.indexLine: Kevin asked the program to stop treating a tap-and-pick input as the realistic product and break through to a fully automatic bar. The first registered step compares the field's joint beat and downbeat trackers (Beat This!, madmom) with the production detector on the 23 recordings the program holds bar-level truth for, at zero model spend. On the ten modern songs the detector's bar period is strict on three; the trackers reach six or seven, with madmom folded on all ten and the only system to meet the registered decision rule, so the Study 38 automatic re-draft will run on its bar. On the jazz 78s every neural tracker reads the bar the detector halves, and madmom places downbeats within 70 ms on up to 96 percent of bars with counts of 114 of 114, 52 of 53 and 126 of 125, the Study 34 tempo-following result with no declared tempo supplied. Compound meter is where the trackers lose: Beat This has no 6/8 class and reads both compound songs as three-beat bars, while the detector's automatic mode gets one of them exactly, which makes Study 35's failure there the declared-tempo units bug alone.

table.summary: Per system: bar period strict and folded, meter class, downbeat phase and bar counts, on the ten modern songs and the acoustic-era six

body.heading: The Question
body.html: Thirty-five studies in, the program's standing read was that the automatic detector's tempo and meter are the weak link and that a visitor who taps the tempo and picks the meter is the realistic product. Kevin rejected that framing and asked for a research pass on what had not been tried. The resulting proposal reframed the target: the product needs the bar (its period, its grouping, and where it starts), not a tempo number, and the field has spent a decade on exactly that object under the name downbeat tracking. Study 36 is the proposal's first step, registered before any run: the published trackers against the production detector, graded at the bar, on every recording the program already holds truth for.

body.heading: Systems and Truth
body.html: Production is the v0.200 detector port followed by the shipped grid, vote and placement, automatic mode exactly as the product would run it. Against it: Beat This! (ISMIR 2024, MIT weights) in its 78 MB and 8 MB checkpoints with the authors' minimal peak-picking, and the 78 MB model with madmom's dynamic Bayesian postprocessor; madmom's own RNN and DBN downbeat tracker with bars of three or four beats, and an exploratory variant that also allows six; librosa's unseeded tracker as the classical tempo baseline. Truth is the 23-recording union of Studies 34 and 35: five click-exact Badverbs mixes with uniform downbeat grids, three JAAH jazz 78s with beat-aligned downbeats and bar counts, the hymn and the waltz with tempo from the self-similarity instrument, ten Josh Woodward songs at the artist's declared tempo and meter (a 6/8 bar being two dotted quarters), and three meter-only slots. Graders are mechanical and unit-tested: bar period strict within 4 percent or folded at a metrical ratio, meter class, downbeat F-measure within 70 ms where time truth exists, bar counts on the 78s.

body.heading: The Modern Ten
body.html: Bar period strict, folded, and meter right, of ten: production 3, 7, 8; Beat This final 6, 9, 8; Beat This small 7, 8, 8; madmom 7, 10, 8. The registered decision rule (strict on seven, folded on all ten, meter on eight) is met by madmom and by no Beat This variant, so the automatic-mode re-draft registered as Study 38 will run on madmom's bar. The misses are instructive. Every system reads goodbye-to-spring, declared 240, at 120, the registered counter-case that is a convention rather than an error. The small Beat This model's one clean failure is a three-beat bar on that same straight 4/4 song. And im-letting-go, declared 76, comes back at double tempo from every tracker, the other direction of the same convention.

body.heading: The 78s and the Phase
body.html: On livery-stable-blues every neural tracker reads the 1.46 second bar that production reads as 2.71; on dippermouth 1.28 against 2.56; on st-louis 3.53 to 3.58 against 6.12. madmom places the downbeat within 70 ms on 96 percent of livery's bars and 66 percent of dippermouth's, with bar counts of 126 against 125 truth, 114 of 114 and 52 of 53, which is Study 34's exploratory tempo-following result delivered by a published system with no declared tempo given to it. Beat This gets the same periods but puts every downbeat on beat three of dippermouth's bars, a half-bar phase error that scores zero on downbeat F while the bars themselves are right; its DBN variant lands st-louis at 53 of 53. The hymn defeats every system, 2.30, 3.01 and 3.33 seconds against 2.47 declared, the recording the field's own literature names as the hard class. Beat This alone names the waltz's three; madmom reads four at half tempo.

body.heading: Compound Meter Cuts the Other Way
body.html: Production's automatic mode gets gravity's 6/8 bar exactly: an eighth-note pulse of 145.9 with triplet subdivision becomes a 2.466 second bar against the true 2.5. Study 35's confidently wrong draft on that song was therefore the declared-tempo units bug alone, and the app's input adapter remains the whole fix there. The trackers are worse than the detector on this class. Beat This has no compound meter in its vocabulary and reads both 6/8 songs as three-beat bars, gravity as three eighths (half the bar) and my-favorite-regret as three beats of two per dotted quarter, a reading that folds to nothing. madmom with a six-beat class names both, then hears sixes in 4/4 jazz. If a tracker replaces the detector for the bar, the detector's subdivision read should keep the meter label.

body.heading: Disclosures and Cost
body.html: On eat-all-the-clocks all five trackers place every downbeat 85 ms after the registered grid, uniformly, which is the registered bar-one offset itself; the 70 ms window makes that a zero for every tracker while production scores 0.99 from the same onset grid that produced the truth. Reported as registered; it is a fixture question and it treats every tracker alike. Prediction tally: P2, P3 and P5 right; P1 wrong on all three clauses (Beat This strict on six, folded on nine, compound on neither); P4 wrong as a conjunction through the dippermouth phase and the halved st-louis bar. Runtime on this VM was 27 to 47 seconds a song for the large Beat This model with the small one not reliably faster on CPU, because the spectrogram front end dominates; browser timing on WebGPU is a Study 38 matter. No model spend.

studies.title: On 261 songs the detector's bar is right one time in three, a tracker's three in four, and the detector's own 6/8 call is its largest error
studies.eyebrow: Study 36b · catalog census · 1,776 cells · $0
studies.indexLine: Every tempo and meter number in this series had rested on at most ten modern songs. Kevin purchased Josh Woodward's complete catalog bundle and authorized a fetch of the 262 song pages that state each song's tempo, meter and feel under CC BY 4.0, giving 261 modern recordings with the author's own numbers and 244 paired instrumental mixes. Registered before any catalog run and scored at zero model spend: the production detector's bar is strict on 36 percent and folded at an octave on 67; Beat This reaches 70 and 90, madmom 66 and 89. On straight 4/4 songs the trackers are at 73 to 76 percent strict against the detector's 38. The detector's largest error class is its own compound-meter call: it names 6/8 on 63 of 223 songs in 4/4, every one through a triplet subdivision read, and 59 of those bars fold to nothing, the Study 11b confound at catalog scale. The instrumental mixes change little for anyone, so the voice is not the problem. Where a tracker disagrees with the page it is usually a bar half the declared length, on songs declared around 72 bpm, which is the merge-safe direction for a chart.
