body.heading: The Corpus
body.html: The artist publishes tempo, key, meter and feel on every song page, and sells the whole catalog as one download rather than offering it as a bulk scrape, so the clean path was to buy it. The bench matched 262 bundle files to pages by normalized title (twelve covers and parodies have no original-song page and are excluded), hashed every file and every zip into the committed manifest, and froze the census one commit before the registration: 223 songs in 4/4 (177 straight, 46 swing), 37 in 6/8 (17 straight, 20 swing), one waltz; declared tempos 40 to 280 with a median of 105. The parse reproduces every Study 35 slot value exactly. Truth is the artist's declaration: four quarters in 4/4, two dotted quarters in 6/8, the convention Study 35 checked against the audio. Declared values are the session click, not beat-aligned time truth, so there is no downbeat phase score here.

body.heading: The Headline Rates
body.html: Regular mixes, bar strict within 4 percent, folded at a metrical ratio, and meter class right: production 36, 67 and 69 percent; Beat This final 70, 90 and 85; Beat This small 69, 90 and 87; madmom 66, 89 and 85. On the 177 straight 4/4 songs the trackers reach 73 to 76 strict and 91 to 93 folded against production's 38 and 64, and madmom names the 4/4 class on every one of them. The 95 percent Wilson interval on Beat This's 4/4 strict rate runs 70 to 81 percent on 223 songs, the first tempo number in the series with an interval worth printing. Swing cost the trackers nothing, 76 against 76, where the registration had predicted a ten-point penalty. The registered decision rule for adopting a tracker's bar outright, 80 percent strict and 95 folded, is met by none; the nearest is Beat This at 76 and 94.

body.heading: The Detector's Own 6/8
body.html: Production names 6/8 on 63 of the 223 songs the artist wrote in 4/4, 56 of them straight. Every one arrives through the subdivision test reading three, and 59 of the 63 bars it then builds fold to no metrical ratio of the truth at all. This is the peaceful-dreams confound that Study 11b found and 11c reproduced synthetically, now at catalog scale: the sub-beat test fires on straight running eighths and the ladder constructs a bar the song does not have. The instrumental mixes show it is not the voice (42 of 208 there). When the detector names 6/8 on a song that is in 6/8, 21 of 37, the bar is strict on two. And its tempo confidence does not separate right from wrong on 261 songs: medians 0.762 against 0.685, with twelve right and eleven wrong detections above the 0.84 line Study 34b had read off fifteen recordings. Study 35's advice to the app, do not ship the refusal, stands at scale.

body.heading: Compound Meter Is Unsolved for Everyone
body.html: On the 37 songs in 6/8 the bar is strict for 8 percent of them under production, 32 to 35 under Beat This, 16 under madmom. Beat This reads them as six beats to the bar on eighteen, three on twelve, and lands at the 3/2 fold on eight, a 4/4 bar laid over a 6/8 song. madmom, with bars of three or four only, never satisfies the class. The one song in 3/4 is named by every tracker and read at a fold by all of them. Compound meter is the class the proposal's later tiers (a harmonic-rhythm witness, band-split accents) are for, and this census gives them 37 songs to be graded on.

body.heading: The Voice Is Not the Problem
body.html: The paired arm asked the separation question without running a separator: the same song with and without the vocal. Beat This fixes 10 of its 74 regular-mix failures when the voice is removed and breaks 11 of its 170 passes; the small model fixes 5 and breaks 6; production's outcome changes on 35 of 244 songs, 14 percent, in both directions. The registered threshold for moving source separation up the list was a 50 percent fix rate. At 14 percent, separation goes back down it and the harmonic-rhythm witness comes first.

body.heading: The Fold Is a Convention, and It Is Merge-Safe
body.html: Of Beat This's 39 readings on 4/4 songs that fold but are not strict, 28 are a bar half the declared length and 8 a bar twice it. The half readings sit on songs declared at a median of 72 bpm; the double readings at 212. The trackers live in the 80 to 160 lane, and the artist's slow and fast declarations are session choices outside it. A grid at half the declared bar is a finer grid, which a chart can merge into the coarser one without losing a chord; the coarser direction, where a bar would have to be split, is three and a half times rarer. The proposal's collapse-safe octave policy, prefer the shorter bar and merge identical neighbours, covers 28 of the 39. Ten songs disagree with their page under all three trackers while the trackers agree with each other within 4 percent (among them a page saying 75 where the trackers say 106, and 124 swing against 164); they are listed in the brief, not re-graded.

body.heading: Predictions and Disclosures
body.html: Mostly wrong in the details, right in the shape: the trackers landed four points under the registered 80 percent strict on straight 4/4 and two under the 95 folded line; the small checkpoint beat the large one on swing meter by eight points where five was the registered margin; the instrumental break rate was 6.5 percent against a predicted 5. Right: madmom within eight points of Beat This on 4/4 and worse on 6/8, the instrumental fix rate under 25 percent, the fold direction, and the interval width. One labelling disclosure: the fold-direction prediction was written in tempo terms (a 240 song read at 120 called the half fold) while the grader's ratio is on the bar, where that same reading is a two; the prediction is scored under its own words and the brief says so. The twelve Study 34 and 35 songs sit inside this corpus and move no rate. The run took five hours of CPU on this VM, not the fourteen the registration estimated, and cost nothing in model spend.

studies.title: Chord changes cannot pick the bar's octave, and a chart drafted at half the bar loses nothing
studies.eyebrow: Study 37 · witness and policy · 1,048 cells · $0.45
studies.indexLine: Study 36b left the automatic bar at 70 percent strict and 90 percent folded: the gap is the metrical octave, a bar half or twice the written length. Study 37 tried the two ways of closing it. A harmonic-rhythm witness that scores candidate bars by how often chord changes land on bar lines is net negative on every base system, fixing 1 of Beat This's 34 folded readings and breaking 30 of its 165 correct ones, because the chord reader emits 60 to 124 changes per song and any stability term votes for the shorter bar. The policy that makes the fold harmless works instead: three songs drafted at half the declared bar grade 20 of 21, 16 of 18 and 33 of 33 roots against 18, 15 and 28 at the declared bar, and merging identical neighbours brings the chart under the declared-grid length. The two 6/8 slots drafted at the adapter's true bar move from confidently wrong to 23 of 26 and 40 of 42, confirming Study 35's units fix where it costs money.

table.summary: Part C: the witness per base system and meter class; part D: the five re-drafts against their Study 35 baselines

body.heading: The Two Instruments
body.html: Part C is a mechanical witness over the 261 regular mixes at zero spend. For each base system (Beat This final and small, madmom, the production detector) the candidate bars are the base bar at the ratios one half, two thirds, one, three halves and two; ChordMini's chord-change times are snapped to the base beat lattice and each candidate is scored at its best phase by the share of bars that start with a change times the share with no change inside, with abstention under eight changes or a margin under a tenth. Part D re-drafts five Study 35 slots through the Study 35 pipeline verbatim with the typed tempo changed to what an automatic grid would hand the product: the three 4/4 near-misses at twice the declared tempo (the trackers' common fold) and the two 6/8 songs at three times the declared dotted-quarter tempo (the input adapter's reading). The new measure is the merged bar count after identical neighbours collapse.

body.heading: The Witness Fails
body.html: On Beat This final's 223 songs in 4/4 the witness fixes one folded reading and breaks thirty correct ones, taking strict from 74 to 61 percent; madmom fixes four and breaks thirty-three; production fixes thirteen and breaks sixteen. It abstains on two thirds of songs, and when it acts it votes for the half bar twenty-six times in seventy-seven. The score profiles show why: the chord reader emits sixty to one hundred twenty-four changes per song, most of them inside the bar as suspensions, passing chords and inversions, so a stability term punishes every longer bar. An unregistered pass that removed segments shorter than a beat or two stayed net negative. The one place it helps is compound meter on madmom and production, where the two-thirds ratio moves six 6/8 songs each from a double bar to the declared bar and breaks none.

body.heading: The Half Bar Is Free
body.html: Drafted at half the declared bar, let-it-in, same-boat and im-letting-go grade 20 of 21, 16 of 18 and 33 of 33 roots against 18, 15 and 28 at the declared bar in Study 34 and 35, and two cross into the good class. The model given twice the bars with half the notes each reads the harmony at least as well. The merged charts run 98, 56 and 51 bars against declared-grid drafts of 120, 74 and 58, because merging identical neighbours also collapses the song's own repeats: a merged chart is a progression, not a bar chart, and its readability is the product's question. The two 6/8 slots drafted at the adapter's true bar move from 16 of 26 and 26 of 42 roots, both confidently wrong in Study 35, to 23 of 26 and 40 of 42, one of them good. Spend 45 cents of a 60 cent fence.

body.heading: Predictions and Disclosures
body.html: Part C: six of seven predictions wrong, in the direction of the witness being useless rather than harmful by less than expected: it fixed one reading, not half of them; broke 18 percent of correct bars, not under 15; left 6/8 unchanged; and the strict bar was among its candidates on 89 percent of songs against a registered 90. Only the abstention rate came in as predicted. Part D: the merged-length, 6/8 and grid-drift predictions were right; the two-root band was wrong under its words because two drafts improved past it and changed class upward. One instrument correction is disclosed: the first witness pass measured the bar from the mean beat interval, which tracker gaps bias and which failed to reproduce Study 36b; that run is preserved in the repository, the runner was corrected to the registered median with a reproduction check, and re-run, with no threshold or prediction changed. The decision for Study 38: draft on the tracker's bar as read, prefer the shorter candidate when two fold into each other, apply no harmonic-rhythm correction, and keep the 6/8 adapter fix.

studies.title: A visitor who types nothing gets a chart as good as one who types the artist's tempo, and free tempo is where the next work is
studies.eyebrow: Study 38 · fully automatic chart · 274 cells · $3.84
studies.indexLine: The first charts drafted with no visitor input at all: a beat tracker's downbeats as the bar lines, its median beat as the tempo, its beats per bar as the meter, the detector's key. On the ten modern songs with artist-chart truth every automatic draft lands within two roots of the draft made at the artist's declared tempo or above it, eight of ten good, none wrong; the two 6/8 songs that Study 35 charted three bars long per bar come out 24 of 26 and 40 of 42 with no meter typed. On 36 solo acoustic-guitar excerpts (GuitarSet, the player's lead sheet as truth) the automatic grid averages 96 percent roots against 99 on the annotated bars, so the remaining cost on acoustic material is the chord reader, not the bar. On 24 free-tempo voice-and-piano songs (Winterreise) every draft is confidently wrong: the steady-tempo tracker's downbeats drift and the music changes chord one and a half times a bar, more than a one-chord-per-bar chart can carry. The tracker that follows rubato is the one that lost on full-band songs.

table.summary: Per arm: the automatic drafts against their baselines or oracle grids, and the trackers' bars against the annotated bars

body.heading: The Automatic Pipeline
body.html: Bar lines are madmom's downbeats as read (the Study 36 winner on full-band recordings), the tempo its median beat, the meter its beats per bar, the key the production detector's; from the bar lines on, the Study 35 pipeline runs verbatim, with no harmonic-rhythm correction (Study 37) and a bar half the written length accepted as read (Study 37). Three arms, registered before any paid draft with a fence of eight dollars: the ten modern songs with artist-chart truth against their declared-grid baselines; 36 GuitarSet singer-songwriter comping excerpts drafted twice, on the annotated bars and on the tracker's; and the 24 songs of the Schubert Winterreise Dataset's SC06 performance, voice and piano at a free tempo, against the audio-time chord annotation. A zero-cost metrical arm graded madmom and Beat This against the annotated bars on the two proxies, including the dataset's public-domain 1933 performance.

body.heading: Modern Songs: Automatic Equals Typed
body.html: All ten drafts land within two roots of the declared-grid baseline or above it: eight equal or better, two one root under; eight good, none confidently wrong. Gravity and My Favorite Regret, which Study 35 charted three bars long per bar from the artist's own 6/8 tempo, come out 24 of 26 and 40 of 42 roots with nothing typed, because madmom's three-beat bar at the dotted quarter is the bar. Goodbye to Spring stays perfect at a double bar and I'm Letting Go goes from 28 of 33 to 33 of 33 at a half bar, both as Study 37 predicted. The first decision rule fires: automatic mode is the tracker's bar as read, the shorter bar preferred, and the tempo-confidence refusal retired.

body.heading: Acoustic Guitar: The Bar Is Nearly Free
body.html: On the annotated bars the 35 graded drafts average 99 percent roots, 28 good, none wrong; on madmom's bars the 32 graded average 96 percent, 24 good, three confidently wrong, all three on one dense lead sheet. Paired, the tracker grid costs 2.9 points. Qualities sit at 86 to 89 percent on both grids because the players voice sevenths the sheet does not name, so on acoustic material the chord reader is the next target, not the bar. Without drums the trackers swap places: Beat This's bar is strict on 86 percent of excerpts with downbeat F 0.97, madmom's on 61 percent with F 0.69, every madmom miss a half bar.

body.heading: Free Tempo: Both Halves Fail
body.html: Every Winterreise draft is confidently wrong, roots 41 percent against the chord sequence and 67 against the chord at each annotated bar start. Two structural causes. The material changes chord 1.5 times per tracker bar, so a one-chord-per-bar chart is bounded near 50 percent on the sequence truth before any error. And madmom's dynamic Bayesian network, built for steady tempo, does not follow the rubato: downbeat F 0.39 against Beat This's 0.68, the same on the 1933 recording of the same songs. For the acoustic-demo target this sets Study 39: a tracker comparison on free-tempo material with Beat This's downbeats as the lead, and a draft format that carries two chords per bar.

body.heading: Predictions and Disclosures
body.html: Right: all four modern predictions but one clause (My Favorite Regret was predicted to misalign at madmom's three-dotted-quarter bar and did not, because its phrases are six dotted quarters long), the guitar oracle and tracker-grid predictions, and the guitar downbeat prediction. Wrong: Beat This was predicted within ten points of madmom on guitar and was 25 points better; every free-tempo prediction failed, and the tracker ordering reversed. Disclosed: the SC06 audio is CC BY-NC-ND, read from the dataset's license file after download, used unmodified for measurement only and never redistributed, with the public-domain 1933 performance added to the metrical arm for that reason; five of 72 guitar answers came back from the gateway empty or cut off and are labelled refused, and three of them came back empty again on an unregistered retry with the finish reason content filter, so the gateway's safety filter stops the chart draft on three particular excerpts; chord truth on the two proxies is a sequence while a draft carries one chord per bar, the Study 34 convention, with the per-bar bound reported beside it.

studies.title: No tracker follows a free tempo well enough to chart it: Beat This keeps the beats and splits the bars, every DBN keeps the bar and loses the beats
studies.eyebrow: Study 39 · free tempo · 408 cells · $0
studies.indexLine: Eight downbeat systems over 48 performances of Schubert's Winterreise with annotated bars, the proxy for acoustic demos without a fixed tempo, plus three steadily drifting 1930s jazz 78s. Beat This with its minimal peak-picking follows the rubato, finding 86 percent of the annotated downbeats within 70 milliseconds, but places a half bar on 14 of the 48 and a strict bar on only 6. Every Dynamic Bayesian Network, Beat This's own included, does the opposite: it holds a bar length on up to 24 of 48 and loses the beats under it. Loosening madmom's tempo penalty bought half the predicted recall. On steady drift madmom is best by a wide margin. No system was chartable, recall at least 0.8 at the bar or half bar, on more than 11 of 48 against a floor of 36, so no free-tempo tracker is adopted; the next study on this material is the draft format on Beat This's bars.

table.summary: Eight downbeat systems against annotated bars on 48 Winterreise performances and three JAAH 78s

body.heading: The Corpus and the Measure
body.html: The target is a live acoustic demo without a fixed tempo. Until real demos arrive the bench used the Schubert Winterreise Dataset, 24 songs in two recorded editions, a 2006 studio recording and a 1933 one, with every bar annotated, and three steadily drifting jazz 78s from the JAAH annotations as a second kind of free tempo. Eight systems ran at zero model spend: Beat This in its big and small checkpoints with the minimal peak-picking postprocessor, the big one with the madmom Dynamic Bayesian Network added, madmom's own network at four tempo-transition penalties, and madmom allowing bars of six. Each was scored by precision and recall of its downbeats within 70 and 150 milliseconds of the annotated bars, by whether its median bar matched the annotated bar strictly or at a metrical fold, and by a registered chartable test: recall of at least 0.8 with the bar at unity or the half.

body.heading: Two Opposite Failures
body.html: Beat This with peak-picking follows the rubato: the big model finds 86 percent of the annotated downbeats within 70 milliseconds, the small one 75. But each places too many downbeats, precision around a half, and the big model's median bar is half the annotated one on 14 of 48 performances with a strict bar on only 6. Every Dynamic Bayesian Network inverts this. Beat This with the DBN holds a strict bar on 24 of 48 and finds 54 percent of the downbeats; madmom holds 16 to 17 strict bars and finds 37 to 45 percent. Loosening madmom's transition penalty from 100 to 10 raised its recall by 0.08, half the predicted 0.15, and cost it chartable performances. The DBN's trouble on lieder is not the transition cost alone but the assumption of a tempo to transition between.

body.heading: Steady Drift Is Different
body.html: On the three jazz 78s, which drift steadily rather than breathe, the order reverses as predicted: madmom at its default penalty is best by a wide margin, F 0.97 at 150 milliseconds against 0.75 for Beat This, and its bar is strict on all three. The 1933 Winterreise edition decides more than predicted: the small Beat This model loses 0.16 of recall from the 2006 to the 1933 recording and the DBN systems 0.10 to 0.16, while the big peak-picking model and madmom at its default are indifferent. On poor audio the model size matters more than the postprocessor.

body.heading: Predictions and Decision
body.html: Right: the big Beat This model's recall at or above 0.75, the DBN below peak-picking on the lieder, and madmom best on the 78s. Wrong: the loosened penalty's gain, and the two editions agreeing within 0.10 for every system, which held only for the two systems whose numbers were already public. No system was chartable on more than 11 of 48 against a registered floor of 36, so the decision rule adopts no free-tempo tracker. The best available bar lines for the next study are the big Beat This model's at the half-bar fold where it sits, since Study 37 showed half-bar drafts grade no worse, and that study asks the format question: two chords a bar on recordings where the harmony changes 1.5 times a bar.

studies.title: The detector's 6/8 call protects nothing, so dropping it raises its bar on every count, and the finer-bar rule is net negative
studies.eyebrow: Study 40 · detector sweeps · 1,044 cells · $0
studies.indexLine: The app asked the bench three threshold questions about its own tempo detector before shipping rules: which second witness keeps the true 6/8 calls and drops the 63 false ones, whether the triplet test is a threshold away from right, and at what strength of the double-tempo rung the automatic grid should take the finer bar. Swept at zero spend on the 261-song catalog through a probe pinned to the detector on every song. No witness separates true 6/8 from false, but the call carries no bar value to protect: the detector's 6/8 bar is right on 2 of the 21 songs it is right to name, so gating or removing the call raises the strict bar from 95 to 114 songs, the folded bar from 176 to 201 and the meter from 180 to 214 with none made wrong. The triplet test's 56 false straight songs are a different test, not a threshold away. The finer-bar rule breaks two to three bars for every one it fixes at every strength, and no tempo cap rescues it. Study 38's answer stands: a tracker's bar as read.

table.summary: The duple-bar witness and the finer-bar rule swept over the catalog, graded as Study 36b graded the detector

body.heading: The Instrument
body.html: The production port keeps its tempo stage private, so the bench copied the pulse finder, the autocorrelation readers and the meter lean verbatim into a probe that exposes, per song, the pulse before the compound re-pick, the re-pick, and the autocorrelation at every lag the two subdivision tests and the proposed witnesses read. One extraction per regular mix; every sweep is arithmetic on that file. The registered gate was a reproduction pin: the probe at production thresholds must give the detector's own tempo and meter on every song. It failed twice, on 15 and 16 songs, because the meter lean was read on the detrended envelope at the unrounded tempo where the detector reads the raw envelope at the rounded one; the corrected probe pins 261 of 261 and the earlier extraction is preserved in the repository.

body.heading: The 6/8 Call Protects Nothing
body.html: The duple-bar witness compares the autocorrelation at the compound bar's lags with the straight bar's on every 6/8 call and falls back to the straight meter at the detector's first pulse when the ratio is under r. At every r it drops the 21 true calls faster than the 63 false ones, reaching 4 true against 10 false at r equal to 1. Yet it raises the strict bar from 95 to 114 songs with none made wrong, and never naming 6/8 at all is within two songs of that on every count. The reason was already in Study 36b: when the detector names 6/8 on a true 6/8 song its bar is strict on 2 of 21, so every 6/8 call is a wrong bar whether the meter is right or not. The triplet test's own thresholds cannot help: across 60 cells the best keeps 13 true against 45 false, and turning the test off leaves 22 false. The bench's advice to the app is to stop emitting 6/8 from the subdivision read while the detector remains in the scan offer, and Study 38 reached the same place from the other side, where a tracker's bar charted both 6/8 songs good with no meter label.

body.heading: The Finer-Bar Rule Fails on the Detector
body.html: Taking the double-tempo rung when its strength is at least s breaks two to three bars for every one it fixes at every s from 0.6 to 1.0 and leaves the strict count below the baseline's 95 everywhere. The rung's strength does not mark the half-bar readings, and neither does tempo: the 37 songs the rule would fix have detected tempos from 70 to 149 against 80 to 170 for the 95 already right, so a cap at 90 fixes 19 and endangers 13 and a cap at 100 fixes 29 and endangers 29. The Study 36b observation the rule came from was about the trackers' half bars, which are merge-safe because a tracker's beat is the beat; the detector's double rung is the wrong octave as often as the right one.

body.heading: Predictions and Decision
body.html: Right: no triplet-test cell separates the populations, and the best witness cell raises the strict bar by at least ten songs. Wrong: a witness keeping at least fifteen true 6/8 calls at ten or fewer false ones, and a net-positive finer-bar threshold. Wrong by two points: 78 percent of the fixable songs sit under 100 bpm against a registered 80. No cell met its registered floor, so the decision rule returns Study 38's recommendation alone, a tracker's bar as read on full-band material, and the bench adds, outside the floors and labelled so, that the detector should not name 6/8 from the subdivision read. Both answers were written back into the app's brief in its repository.

studies.title: Beat This small carries the automatic chart on all ten songs, and the browser-sized export turns out to be the right weights at the wrong window
studies.eyebrow: Study 41 · one tracker · 112 cells · $2.01
studies.indexLine: The app wants to ship one beat tracker for the fully automatic chart and named Beat This small, a 10 MB model with a browser port. The bench redrafted the ten modern songs of Study 38 on its bars as read, and on the big checkpoint's. The small model's drafts are within two roots of madmom's on all ten, seven identical and two better, with none confidently wrong, so the app's rule passes and the chart ships on one tracker. Two of its bars were half bars and cost nothing. The three draft holds were censused against the 46 drafts on a tracker's bars: the detected-grid hold holds everything, the drift hold holds 17 and comes out, the thin-transcription hold fires on nothing and keeps its earlier evidence. The recipe is pinned with hashes, and the 10 MB ONNX export is found to carry the identical weights but to break past 300 frames, so the 5-second chunks it forces make it a different tracker from the 30-second model the census measured.

table.summary: Roots right of bearing on the ten modern songs, four grids; the three draft holds; the ONNX export against the package

body.heading: The Draft on Beat This's Bars
body.html: Study 38 drafted the ten modern songs on madmom's bars. This study ran the same pipeline, Basic Pitch notes, per-bar chord hints, the chart-drafting prompt and the sequence grader against the artist's charts, with the bar lines a Beat This tracker's downbeats as read, its median beat the tempo, its beats per bar the meter. The small checkpoint's drafts are within two roots of madmom's on 10 of 10, identical on seven songs and two roots better on two, with eight graded good and the same two as on every grid just under the quality threshold. The big checkpoint misses the app's rule on one song by three roots, still good, where its bars are the most fragmented of the twenty cells. Two of the small model's ten bars were half bars and the drafts on them scored 42 of 42 and 43 of 43, as Study 37 predicted half bars would.

body.heading: The Policy With Nothing Typed
body.html: Operationally: every tracker bar is a chart bar, identical neighbours merged afterwards; the tempo is sixty over the median beat interval; the meter is the rounded ratio of median bar to median beat. Nothing is compared when nothing is declared, and the shorter bar is kept when a declared bar exists and the tracker's is half of it. Study 38's label rule had one blind spot, now measured: a modal count of six beats to the bar on a 6/8 song was labelled 4/4 at 143 bpm on a bar that was the true 6/8 bar. The draft did not suffer because the bars were right. The replacement labels from the modal count, six meaning 6/8 at the tempo divided by three, which lands on the declared 48 exactly.

body.heading: The Holds and the Recipe
body.html: Against the 46 Study 38 drafts on a tracker's bars, the detected-grid hold holds every automatic draft and so filters nothing. The drift hold would hold 17, twelve of them good, and catches one of the three confidently wrong drafts; sixteen of its seventeen sit at a metrical fold of the declared bar, the shorter bar the policy keeps, so it comes out. The thin-transcription hold fires on nothing, the sparsest draft having five notes a bar, so this corpus neither confirms nor refutes it and it keeps its Study 34b evidence. The recipe the bench ran is written down with checkpoint sizes and hashes, the spectrogram parameters, the 30-second chunking, the minimal peak-picking postprocessor and the wall time, about six seconds per minute of audio for the small model on the bench VM.

body.heading: The ONNX Export
body.html: The bench's own 10 MB ONNX export of the small model, used in Study 10, disagrees with the torch package on the same ten songs, downbeat agreement 0.51 to 0.78 with bar counts off by up to 82. Fed the same spectrogram in 250-frame chunks, its frame logits equal the package's to the second decimal with identical peak counts, so the weights are the same. The export's attention breaks past about 300 frames, which Study 10's runner had recorded and worked around with 5-second chunks, and a tracker with five seconds of context is a different tracker from one with thirty. Study 10's beat numbers were the short-window tracker; Studies 36 to 41 are the long one. The browser port must be an export that runs at the reference window, verified against the package's logits before any census number is trusted. Predictions: three right, two wrong, one unscored; spend overran the two-dollar pre-draft fence by one cent on the last registered draft.

studies.title: The browser-sized tracker export is fixed, reproduces the measured system exactly, and runs fast enough for the browser
studies.eyebrow: Study 42 · the export · 29 cells · $0
studies.indexLine: Study 41 had found the bench's 10 MB export of Beat This small carried the right weights but broke past 300 frames. The cause turned out to be the rotary position embedding's cache, which an exporter bakes at the traced length. Two new exports avoid it: one traced at the reference 1500-frame window and one with the cache off and a dynamic length. Both match the Python package's frame logits to float32 noise, and the static one, run through the reference inference, reproduces the package's beats and downbeats exactly on all ten modern songs. Timed on a 30-second chunk, ONNX Runtime on CPU matches torch at four threads, and ONNX Runtime Web's WebAssembly backend takes 4.5 seconds single-threaded, about nine seconds per minute of audio, so the registered rule places the tracker in the browser behind a lazy load with the server as fallback.

table.summary: The two exports, their agreement with the package, and model time per 30-second chunk by runtime

body.heading: The Cause
body.html: The Beat This model positions its attention with rotary embeddings from a library that caches the position frequencies in a buffer and slices the first n rows on every call. When an exporter traces the model at some input length, that slice becomes a constant of that length, so any longer input is rotated with the wrong frequencies and the attention degrades. The export the bench inherited had been traced short, which is why Study 10 could only run it in 5-second chunks and why Study 41 found it tracking differently from the 30-second model. The fix is to trace at the inference length, or to turn the cache off and export with a dynamic length. The bench did both.

body.heading: Verified to the Package
body.html: Frame logits from the two exports against the torch package differ by at most seven hundred-thousandths on three songs, the dynamic export at 750, 1500 and 3000 frames alike. The static export was then run through the reference inference in numpy, 1500-frame chunks stitched with a six-frame border and the minimal peak-picking postprocessor, and compared with the package's own beats and downbeats on the ten modern songs: F 1.000 on both, with identical counts on all ten. Where the old export had read 87 downbeats on Cherubs, this one reads 169, the same as the package. This export is the system of Studies 36 to 41.

body.heading: Timed, and Placed
body.html: On a 30-second chunk the torch package takes 0.56 seconds on the bench VM's sixteen cores and ONNX Runtime on CPU 0.54 at four threads, 1.3 on one. ONNX Runtime Web's WebAssembly backend, the app's browser runtime at its pinned version, takes 4.5 seconds on one thread; requesting four threads changed nothing in Node, so that figure is the single-thread floor and a browser with SIMD and threads should improve on it. That is about nine seconds of model time per minute of audio, a four-minute song in roughly 36 seconds, under the registered threshold of fifteen seconds per minute, so the bench recommends the browser behind the lazy load the transcriber already uses, with ONNX Runtime on the server at about one second per minute as the fallback.

body.heading: Predictions and Hand-over
body.html: Right: the static export matches the package at 1500 frames, reproduces its beats on the ten songs, the dynamic export matches at other lengths, and WebAssembly comes in under the thresholds. Wrong: ONNX Runtime at its default thread count is one and a half times slower than torch, reaching parity only at four threads. The export is handed to the app with its hash and a reproduction script, together with the four parts of the port: the log mel front end already verified in numpy, the chunking, the postprocessor, and the tempo and meter derivations from Study 41. The exports are not committed, being binaries reproducible from the checkpoint; their hashes are.

studies.title: Two cells a bar on fast-moving harmony: the dense guitar sheet was a quality gap, and the lieder lift but stay wrong
studies.eyebrow: Study 43 · the draft format · 40 drafts · $1.54
studies.indexLine: The two failures left on the automatic chart looked like one failure: a one-chord-per-bar draft cannot score a bar with two chords. The study drafted twelve GuitarSet takes and the eight shortest Winterreise songs twice each on Beat This small's bars, once as read and once with each bar split at its middle beat. The premise was wrong on the guitar: the dense sheet is one chord a bar with repeats, its roots are already right on the tracker's bars, and what holds five of six takes below good is chord quality. On the lieder the half grid lifted the root median from 0.36 to 0.58 and left every song confidently wrong. One song reached good on the tracker's bars as read, the first Winterreise song to do so. No grid change recommended.

body.heading: The Premise, and What Was Wrong With It
body.html: Study 38's three confidently wrong guitar drafts all came from one GuitarSet sheet with fourteen chord positions in sixteen bars, and the Winterreise songs average a chord change and a half a bar. The draft writes one chord per cell and the pipeline hands it one cell per bar, so the bench registered a controlled test: the same pipeline, the same tracker's bars, each item drafted on the bar as read and on the bar split at the beat nearest its middle. The sheet turned out to be one chord a bar with two repeats, so the format was never its ceiling. Its earlier failures were madmom's bar lines; on Beat This small's bars as read, four of six takes score every root right and the fifth misses two.

body.heading: The Guitar Gap Is Quality
body.html: What keeps five of the six dense-sheet takes below good is the quality column: seven of eleven on four takes and two of eleven on one. The sheet carries a dominant seventh and two minor chords, and the drafts write the roots and miss the colours. Splitting the bar changed nothing on eight of the twelve takes, lifted two, and lowered none. The acoustic guitar question therefore moves from the tracker and the grid to the drafting prompt and the per-bar hints, where the chord quality is decided.

body.heading: The Lieder Lift and Stay Wrong
body.html: On the eight shortest Winterreise songs the half grid lifted five, lowered two, and moved the root median from 0.36 to 0.58, two hundredths short of the registered prediction. Every song remained confidently wrong on the half grid, and one dropped hard where 283 cells of four tenths of a second were more than the draft could hold together. The format was part of the ceiling on fast-moving harmony and the audio and the truth are the rest. Unlooked for, one song drafted good on the tracker's bars as read, where the same recording on madmom's bars had scored eighteen of forty-one: the first Winterreise song to reach good in the program, with nothing typed.

body.heading: Decision and Disclosures
body.html: The half grid lifted seven of twenty items and lowered two, so the registered rule recommends no grid change: two cells a bar cost twelve percent more input and buy nothing where chords change by the bar. Three of the forty drafts stopped at the gateway's content filter with empty text, each at the bar grid while the same audio drafted normally at the half grid; they are counted as drafts, left ungraded and not retried. Spend was $1.54 against a $3 fence. One prediction right and three wrong, one of those by two hundredths.

studies.title: Two rules on the tracker's bars, measured: joining is a wash with one clear win, and the steady share enriches without separating
studies.eyebrow: Study 44 · grid rules · 891 cells · $0.35
studies.indexLine: The app now draws its generated draft on Beat This small's downbeats with two rules from five of its own recordings: adjacent half bars are joined, and a reading whose bars do not settle on one beat count is not used. The bench ported both rules verbatim, pinned them to the app's tests, and measured them over the 261-song census, the Woodward songs, the app's five recordings and the Study 43 guitar takes. Joining moves the bar count toward the artist's count about as often as away, but rescues a 6/8 song the steadiness rule would otherwise reject. The steady share removes more right readings than wrong at the app's threshold and misses the one bad draft. The 3/4 at 224 that tripped the rule trips the big checkpoint too.

table.summary: What each steadiness measure removes at each threshold on the census, and what joining does to the bar count

body.heading: The Rules, Ported
body.html: The app's grid code was ported line for line and pinned to its own thirteen test cases, so the bench measured the rule the app ships and not a reading of it. All five of the app's dev recordings were already in the bench's corpus with package readings committed, and the app's beats-per-bar table matched those readings count for count on all five, which answers the port comparison at the bar level before any new work.

body.heading: Joining
body.html: Over the census, joining moves the tracker's bar count toward the declared count on 73 songs and away on 61; among the 180 songs the tracker reads at the declared level it is 44 to 36, with the mean count error falling from 8.7 to 6.1 percent. Two of the app's own five moved toward and two away, the latter two having been under the declared count before joining, so their joined pairs were by count real bars. The clear win is a 6/8 song the tracker reads as bars of three and six by turns: joining turns it into 94 bars against 94 declared and lifts its steady share from 0.46 to 0.84, without which a good draft fails the second rule. The bench's reading is to keep joining, because its failure is cheaper than its success is valuable.

body.heading: The Steady Share
body.html: At the app's threshold the share removes 35 census readings, 13 with the bar wrong at every fold and 22 with it right at some fold, so it enriches for a wrong bar without separating. Among the 22 drafts the bench holds on this tracker's bars it removes two sound drafts and misses the one confidently wrong draft, whose share is 0.93. A fold-tolerant share and the beat interval's coefficient of variation were swept beside it and did no better at any threshold. The registered criterion lands on 0.7, which the bench reports and does not like; its labelled judgment is 0.4, the least that keeps the one chaotic reading off the chart while keeping both good 6/8 drafts.

body.heading: The Fast Waltz
body.html: The 3/4 at 224 beats per minute is not a weakness of the small checkpoint: the big one fails the same rule with the same beat and a different modal bar, and only the dynamic Bayesian postprocessor, like madmom, reads it steadily, at half the declared tempo. The program's other 3/4 stands under both checkpoints, the census's one 3/4 is steady, and its seventeen fastest songs have a median share of 0.88. Fast is not the problem; this song's bar is. The fold-tolerant share tells the case apart from the small checkpoint's output alone on this corpus; the beat interval's variation does not.

body.heading: Addendum: Joining and the Chords
body.html: With the approved spend of thirty-five cents, the four Woodward songs where joining removes four or more bar lines were drafted again on the joined grid. All four scored identically to the drafts on the bars as read in roots, qualities and class, with five, five, four and twenty-four fewer bars. Joining changes the chart's bar count and not its chords, so the recommendation to keep it rests on the bar count alone. The port comparison closed the same day: the app delivered its stored beats for the five recordings, and every beat and downbeat equals the package's reading of the same mix to the frame, 1,772 beats and 478 downbeats with no offset, so the app's port is the measured system on real audio and not only on the synthetic fixture.

studies.title: Chord quality on the one-chord-a-bar sheet: the hint carries most of the loss, and a style-neutral clause recovers some of it
studies.eyebrow: Study 45 · chord quality · 46 cells · $1.46
studies.indexLine: Study 43 left the dense GuitarSet sheet with its roots right and its qualities wrong. This study first attributed every lost quality position in Study 43's guitar drafts to its cause: most sit on bars where the chord model's hint was already wrong, since the model does not hear the half-diminished chord, and the rest are power chords on two thin takes. It then replaced the one clause of the production prompt that asks the model to think like a rock musician with a style-neutral instruction about chord quality, pinned to differ in nothing else, and drafted the twelve guitar takes and the ten modern songs. Qualities rose on six takes and fell on one, the only confidently wrong draft on the shipped tracker's bars became good, the half-diminished was named in seven of twelve drafts, and the modern songs lost nothing. Power chords persisted on the thin takes. Reported without a recommendation by the registered rule; the bench's labelled judgment favours the clause.

table.summary: Where the quality was lost, and the paired drafts under production's clause and the quality clause

body.heading: Where the Quality Goes
body.html: For each of Study 43's 24 guitar cells the bench recomputed the per-bar hints with the same chord model, took the sheet's chord at each bar as truth, and classed every quality-bearing bar by what the hint and the draft did. On the dense sheet at the bar grid, 25 of the 40 lost positions are bars where the hint's quality family was already wrong; the model followed the hint on fourteen and wrote a third family on eleven. Thirteen are power chords on one take, and two are bars where the model lost a right hint. The chord model's vocabulary does carry the half-diminished, a correction made the same day, but the model does not hear it on these bars, so every such bar arrives with a wrong hint.

body.heading: The Clause
body.html: The production system prompt tells the model to think like a rock musician reading a chart, prefer simple progressions over exotic spellings, and expect power chords and sus chords. The variant replaces that clause with an instruction to name the quality the notes support, a seventh when the seventh sounds, a plain triad when it does not, and a power chord only when neither third sounds, and is pinned by test to differ from production in nothing else. Both the guitar takes and the ten modern songs were drafted under it on the shipped tracker's bars, the modern songs as the guard against a clause that helps a jazz sheet and hurts a rock chart.

body.heading: What Moved
body.html: On the ten paired guitar takes, qualities rose on six and fell on one, roots fell on none, and the one confidently wrong draft on Beat This small's bars became good with its half-diminished named. Across all twelve takes five drafts are good under the clause against three of the ten production drafts that answered, and the half-diminished is spelled in seven of twelve where production spelled it in three of ten. Power chords did not retreat: five drafts carry one against three before, the two thin takes among them. The modern songs changed in nothing that matters: one quality count up by one, one root count down by two with the class unchanged, eight good drafts before and after.

body.heading: Decision and Disclosures
body.html: The registered rule required qualities up on six takes and two more good drafts; good rose by one, so the registered outcome is a report without a recommendation, and the runner's own summary line, which used a looser condition and printed a recommendation, is corrected in the brief. The bench's labelled judgment favours the clause on the evidence and names the chord model's accuracy on the half-diminished as the larger remaining gap, which Study 46 measures across all of GuitarSet. Two guitar takes whose production drafts had stopped at the gateway's content filter drafted normally under the new clause; the bench records that and draws no causal line from two cases. Spend was $1.46 against a $2.50 fence; predictions P1, P3 and P4 right, P2 and P5 wrong.
